sentences.text: The notes continued for two more weeks.
Simone was the courier.
Sometimes he carried three or four in a day.
Sometimes only one.
Both old men began to give him small treats — sometimes a piece of candy, sometimes a fig from the tree in their back yards.
He accepted them.
It felt like the fair thing.
In the third week, one of the messages was different.
Signor Marco handed Simone a folded paper and said, out loud, "Tell him — please — I would like to have coffee together on the day of the Assumption of Mary.
In the small square, by the church.
Not at the café.
Somewhere quiet.
If he wants." Simone nodded.
He carried the paper.
He also carried the message.
Bruno received both.
Bruno closed his eyes for a long moment.
Then he said to Simone, "Tell him yes.
Tell him — I have been waiting for him to ask.
Tell him — I will be there." And Simone carried that back to Marco.
Marco stood at his door for a moment.
Then he said, in a voice that had a small crack in it, "Thank you, Simone."
The Assumption of Mary was on the fifteenth of August.
It was a warm evening.
The whole village was in the streets.
There were candles.
There was music.
There was a procession.
Aunt Rosa went with Simone.
They walked through the crowds.
They watched the procession.
Aunt Rosa knew everyone and stopped to talk to everyone.
Simone was distracted.
He kept looking around.
He saw them at eight-thirty.
Signor Bruno was sitting on a small stone bench at the edge of the small square by the church.
Signor Marco was sitting beside him.
They were not looking at each other.
They were both looking at the church.
But they were sitting together.
On the same bench.
For the first time in forty-three years.
Simone stopped.
He did not want to bother them.
He watched from far off.
Aunt Rosa noticed.
She followed his eyes.
She saw the two brothers on the bench.
She stopped talking mid-sentence to whoever she was talking to.
She said, softly, "Simone.
Look at that." Simone said, "Yes.
I see." Aunt Rosa turned to him.
She said, "Simone.
Did you have something to do with this." And Simone said, "A little.
I carried some notes." And Aunt Rosa did not say anything for a long moment.
Then she said, "Well.
Then you have done a very good thing this summer."
Simone and Aunt Rosa watched them from the far side of the square.
Bruno and Marco sat on the bench for maybe an hour.
They did not say much.
Simone could see, sometimes, that one of them was talking, and the other was listening.
Then the other was talking, and the first was listening.
They did not touch.
But they were sitting together, and they were talking, and that was more than forty-three years' worth.
The notes continued for the rest of Simone's visit.
But now the two brothers also went for walks together sometimes, in the evening, when it was cool.
They did not talk to each other in public in the daytime yet — that was too big a step, Simone understood — but they walked in the evenings.
And sometimes, in the very early morning, Simone would see Marco cross the alley to Bruno's house, and Bruno would open the door before Marco could knock.
They would go inside together for a while.
When Simone left in early September, both of them came out to say goodbye.
They stood side by side in the alley, though not touching.
Bruno said, "Thank you, Simone.
You did what neither of us could do.
We will not forget it." Marco said, "Come back next summer.
Come every summer.
You will always have a place with us." Simone hugged both of them, one after the other.
Aunt Rosa was crying a little.
They drove down the road out of the village.
Simone looked back once.
Bruno and Marco were still standing together in the alley.
They were watching the car go.
Bruno raised his hand in a wave.
Marco raised his.
Simone came back the next summer.
Bruno and Marco were sitting together at the café at three in the afternoon, at one table instead of two.
Nobody in the village had said anything about it.
Everyone had just noticed.
Everyone had just adjusted.
That was how these things happened in a small village.
Simone had helped his aunt with the tomatoes.
He had visited Bruno and Marco every evening.
He had felt that this was — that this was how things should be.
Bruno died in the winter that Simone was fifteen.
He died in his sleep, peacefully.
Marco lived another six years after that.
Simone came for the funeral.
When he arrived at the village, Marco was already at the church.
Marco was very small and very old now.
When he saw Simone, he came over and hugged him for a long time.
He said, into Simone's shoulder — Simone was now taller than Marco was — "Thank you, Simone.
You gave me those years with him.
You gave both of us those years.
I have thanked God for you every single day.
I will keep thanking God for you until I go too." And Simone did not know what to say.
He said, "I only carried the notes, Signor Marco." And Marco said, "Simone.
I am eighty-four years old.
Some of the most important things people do in their lives are only carrying notes.
Remember that."
